name: Tagbanwa
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: The only sweep item for tagb1258 (Warner 1979, 'Walking on two feet') is a UH Manoa anthropology dissertation (Glottolog hhtype ethnographic) and is irrelevant to stress.org was blocked, so the sweep fell back to open repositories (sealang, zorc.net, Glottolog, archive.org, Wikipedia) plus files already fetched sources in this audit. The best first-hand statement read is Zorc 1977:218 (own Aborlan data, n. 8 p. 287): Palawano, Aborlan and Agutaynen 'do not have contrastive word accent', backed by Zorc's review of Thiessen 1981 (accent differences in Aborlan idiolectal, from Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata; Thiessen 1981:10 says no Palawan variety distinguishes words by accent alone, accent on one of the last two syllables in the southern varieties). Green 1979 (PL A-50, newly fetched sources), Hussey 1966, Reid 1971 entry 41 and Zorc 2023 are silent. Language is not in the catalog; suggested coding: no contrastive word stress (position unspecified). Acquisition priorities: Thiessen 1980/1981 (medium; OCLC 702398688) and Hussey 1965 (medium).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Aborlan Tagbanwa has no contrastive (phonemic) word accent: unlike Bisayan and Tagalog, words are not distinguished by stress placement. The source does not state where non-contrastive prominence falls. Second-hand (Thiessen 1981:10 as quoted in Zorc's review, on file): in the Palawan languages accent falls on one of the last two syllables of the word and is never contrastive; Zorc's review adds that in his own Aborlan data accent differences are idiolectal and induced by Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata.
new_statements.exceptions: Zorc's review of Thiessen (p. 109): apparent accent contrasts in Aborlan, Brooke's Point Palawano and Batak 'are the result of mimicry of Tagalog or Bisayan forms known to and by individual speakers' and 'often differ from one idiolect to another'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('contrastive word accent'); a one-sentence remark in a comparative study of Bisayan, based on the author's own Aborlan field data cross-checked against Reid 1971; no citation forms or examples given for Aborlan. Thiessen's 'last two syllables' rule (second-hand) is stated for suffixed and unsuffixed words alike.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: Zorc 1977's 'Aborlan' = Aborlan Tagbanwa [tbw] (his language list p. 25 no. 26: 'Aborlan [Tagbanwa], Aborlan (area), southern Palawan'; p. 287 n. 8 names it 'Aborlan Tagbanwa'). Reid 1971 entry 41 represents the dialect of barrio Cabigaan, Aborlan, Palawan (Hussey data). Distinct from Central Tagbanwa [tgt] (Glottolog cent2091; Scebold 2003) and Calamian/Kalamian Tagbanwa [tbk] (Kalamianic), both of which are also called 'Tagbanwa' in the literature; Thiessen 1981 groups Aborlan Tagbanwa with Batak as North Palawan.

new_statements.reading: First-hand (Zorc's own Aborlan field data): Aborlan Tagbanwa has no contrastive/phonemic word accent, i.e. no lexical stress contrasts. Placement of non-contrastive stress is not stated. Corroborated by Zorc's review of Thiessen 1981 (offprint 044, p. 109): accent differences in Aborlan 'are the result of Tagalog or Bisayan superstrata and often differ from one idiolect to another', and Thiessen 1981:10 (quoted there) says that in none of the Palawan varieties are words distinguished by accent alone, with accent on one of the last two syllables in the South Palawan varieties. A fixed-position statement for Aborlan itself would need Thiessen 1980/1981 or Hussey 1963/1965, neither of which is online.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David (c. 1984-1986). Review of Thiessen, Henry Arnold, Phonological reconstruction of Proto-Palawan (Anthropological Papers 10, Manila: National Museum, 1981). Journal offprint pp. 109-111 (venue not printed on the offprint; zorc.net offprint no. 044).
sources.quote: Accent is not marked because it is purportedly not phonemic, although the author's statement of this is somewhat confusing: 'Word accent in Q[uezon], B[rooke's] P[oint], C[anipaan], and M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms. ... In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written' (10). ... However, my own data on Aborlan, Brooke's Point, and Batak indicate that accent differences are the result of Tagalog or Bisayan superstrata and often differ from one idiolect to another. Hence, Proto-Palawan probably had lost PPH accent
sources.note: Second first-hand statement by Zorc: accent differences in Aborlan are idiolectal and due to Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata, i.e. no native contrastive accent. Quotes Thiessen 1981:10 that accent is non-contrastive in all seven Palawan varieties and falls on one of the last two syllables in the South Palawan varieties (Aborlan is not in that named list).
